teaching cards · Socratic self-examination · about 5 min

Whose Hut Is It, Anyway?

Two scholars use the same 100-year-old story about a philosopher's cabin to open books that disagree about whether you can ever separate a good idea from a bad person.

Background

In the 1920s, the German philosopher Martin Heidegger wrote much of his most famous work in a small three-room cabin in Germany's Black Forest. He called it die Hütte, the hut. There was no electricity or running water. Working there, away from modern life, Heidegger developed an idea that still shapes how people think about technology: a tool that works well disappears from our attention. We only notice it when it breaks, and breaking suddenly reveals everything that depended on it.

Two recent scholars use this same story to open very different books, and they disagree about what it means.

Sven Nyholm is a philosopher working in analytic philosophy, a tradition that judges an argument mostly by its logic: is it valid, is it well-supported, largely apart from who made it or when. His 2023 textbook, This Is Technology Ethics, opens with Heidegger's hut to introduce students to the basics of what technology even is.

Edward Jones-Imhotep is a historian of technology. His field is built on historicism: the idea that you cannot fully understand an idea without understanding the specific time, place, and politics that produced it. His 2026 book, The Broken Machine, closes with a chapter called “Beyond Heidegger’s Hut,” using the same story to challenge the very idea Nyholm treats as a starting point.

Both scholars know that Heidegger joined the Nazi Party in 1933, the year Hitler came to power in Germany. That fact isn’t in dispute. What they disagree about is what follows from it.

This is a good test case precisely because it’s hard. It would be easy to say a bad person can never have a good idea, or that a good idea is always good no matter who has it. Almost nobody actually believes either of those things once you push on them. Before you read further, notice which one you were leaning toward just now, and hold onto that. The point of this card is not to tell you which scholar is right. It’s to make you notice the rule you were already using to judge Heidegger, and ask whether you’d apply that same rule consistently to everyone else you read.

The tension

Nyholm’s move: separate the person from the idea. He writes:

“There are also philosophical reasons to start with Heidegger’s discussion, despite whatever flaws Heidegger himself might have had as a person, at least during certain stages of his life.”

Nyholm, This Is Technology Ethics, sec. 1.1

He even notices that Heidegger liked old tools better than new ones:

“Heidegger himself tended to romanticize the past… a sharp distinction between modern technologies… and more traditional technologies.”

sec. 1.1

For Nyholm, that’s just a detail about Heidegger’s personality. It doesn’t damage the argument. This is the classic move of analytic philosophy: an argument stands or falls on its logic, so a flawed person can still hand you a sound argument, the same way a bad cook can still hand you a correct recipe.

Jones-Imhotep’s move: the detail is the problem. Heidegger’s examples, a well, a peasant’s plow, were not neutral. He skipped over the short circuits and factory breakdowns actually happening in the cities around him and chose old, rural tools instead:

“The archaic technologies he pressed into the service of revelation were no innocent philosophical props. Heidegger knew how they hailed a mythical German past rooted in romantic nationalism and its racist conceptions of volk and social order.”

Jones-Imhotep, The Broken Machine, p. 151

For Jones-Imhotep, even Heidegger’s most famous claim, that breaking reveals the truth about tools, was not timeless:

“If anything made that assertion both possible and plausible in the 1920s, it was an unacknowledged cultural history rather than a transhistorical truth.”

p. 153

This is the classic move of historicism: an argument doesn’t float free of its examples. If the examples are doing political work, then judging the argument on “logic alone” quietly lets that political work go unexamined. Nyholm and Jones-Imhotep are not just disagreeing about Heidegger. They are disagreeing about what an argument even is, and whether it can be cleanly separated from the specific illustrations a person used to make it.

Question

Can you take Heidegger’s idea seriously without also taking his politics seriously?

The moral, unresolved

The examples a thinker picks are not just illustrations. Sometimes the politics live inside the examples themselves, and there is no clean way to pull the two apart.

Bold terms inside direct quotations are my editorial flags for further reading, not emphasis in the original text.
